bias

BYE-uhs · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Bias is a prejudice or leaning that unfairly favors one side.

The referee was accused of bias after every close call went to the home team.

Example

The survey showed bias: its questions were worded so that almost any answer sounded like support for the new stadium.

The survey wasn't even-handed -- its wording quietly favored one side of the issue before anyone even answered. That built-in unfair leaning is bias.

How bias sits among its neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

prejudice

prejudice: an unfair opinion formed before knowing the facts

favoritism

favoritism: unfairly preferring one person or side

Antonyms

impartiality

impartiality: treating all sides equally

fairness

fairness: equal, just treatment

How Strong Is It?

preference → bias → prejudice

preference vs. bias

preference vs. bias: A preference is a harmless liking -- bias goes further: the leaning is unfair, and it can warp judgments that should be even-handed.

prejudice vs. bias

prejudice vs. bias: Prejudice is stronger and uglier than bias -- a judgment locked in before the facts, often aimed at a whole group of people.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — biais: a slant; an oblique line (the word's French source) (French (earlier origin uncertain))

Put it together: English borrowed bias from French biais, 'a slant.' Modern English keeps only the mental slant: a judgment that leans unfairly toward one side. For a literal physical tilt, English uses a different word -- slant -- not bias.

Use the root in a new word: unbiased: Jurors are told to stay unbiased until they have heard every piece of evidence.

Strength Check

Word Choice

On the ISEE, bias means an unfair leaning in judgment -- a judge, a hiring panel, a news report, or a study can show bias. It is not a physical tilt or lean: a crooked shelf has a slant, not a bias. Watch for the adjective form, biased.
